A Dedication at Mayanot in Memory of Rabbi Yankel Kranz

In a moving ceremony at the Mayanot World Center, Menachem and Dina Kranz dedicated the main mezuzah of the Beit Midrash in honor of Menachem’s father, Rabbi Yaakov Noach “Yankel” Kranz. Full Story

August 10, 2026 – 27 Av 5786
Share WhatsApp Facebook Twitter Gmail

0:00 / 2:38
Instaread

In a moving ceremony at the Mayanot World Center, Menachem and Dina Kranz dedicated the main mezuzah of the Beit Midrash in honor of Menachem’s father, Rabbi Yaakov Noach “Yankel” Kranz. Full Story

In a moving ceremony at the Mayanot World Center in Jerusalem, Menachem and Dina Kranz dedicated the main mezuzah of the Beit Midrash in honor of his father, Rabbi Yaakov Noach “Yankel” Kranz OBM, the Head Shliach of Virginia.

The dedication carries particular significance as we approach Rabbi Kranz’s 35th yahrzeit on the 6th of Elul. Known as Chodesh HaTeshuvah, Elul is a time to reflect on who we are and who we aspire to become. Rabbi Kranz embodied what it means to be devoted to the Rebbe’s shlichus, to bring Jews closer to Torah, and to recognize the potential within every individual.

Mrs. Fay Kranz opened the event by reading the inscription on the new plaque in the Beit Midrash, joined by many of her children and their families for this momentous occasion.

Gathering alongside the Kranz family were Mayanot students, faculty, and leadership, including Rabbi Kasriel Shemtov, Rabbi Shlomo Gestetner, and Rabbi Yisroel Noach Wichnin, to honor a legacy that continues to inspire Jewish life and learning.

Rivka Marga Gestetner (nee Deitsch), Director of the Mayanot Women’s Program, spoke about the long-intertwined history of the Deitsch and Kranz families, which stretches back to the early days of Danielson, Connecticut.

“Yankel and my mother came from the same small town in Danielson, Connecticut,” she shared. “They were among the very few from that farming community who became religious and went on to raise religious families.”

She recalled Rabbi Kranz’s extraordinary thirst for Torah and his willingness to learn wherever he could. “Rabbi Kranz was a physically tall man, but his thirst to learn was so great that he wasn’t ashamed to sit in a class with young children and learn alongside them. He quickly moved up through the classes until he was able to learn with students his own age and ability.”

“What a legacy for the students of Mayanot to follow in,” Rivka Marga reflected.

That legacy is particularly fitting in the Beit Midrash that now bears his memory. Today, students from around the world walk through the doors of the Mayanot Beit Midrash. They come from many different backgrounds and life experiences, united by a desire to discover something deeper and more meaningful.

Rabbi Kranz’s story is a reminder that growth begins with the humility to learn, the determination to keep growing, and the belief that there is always another level to reach.

Through this meaningful dedication, Menachem and Dina Kranz, together with their family, children, and grandchildren, have ensured that Rabbi Kranz’s example will greet and inspire every student, visitor, and member of the Mayanot community who enters the Beit Midrash.
